transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, what brings me in is… it’s this thing that happens to me when I get into certain tight places. Like if I step into one of those slow elevators, or a little room where the door’s locked, my chest just sort of jumps right away. I don’t mean after I’ve been in there a while, I mean almost immediately, before I’ve even had time to reason with myself.

And then I get this very strong feeling that I need to get back out. It’s like my mind can’t settle on anything else until I know I can leave. I’m 79 now, and I don’t like making a fuss over things, but it’s gotten to where I thought I ought to come talk to somebody, because in those moments I can’t really think straight.
When you’re in one of those situations, is the main thing you’re afraid of being in a closed-in space?

Yes, yes, that’s really it—the closed-in part. I mean, I know in my head that a small storage room or an elevator at a museum isn’t the same thing as being locked up somewhere, but my mind doesn’t seem to care much about that in the moment.

If there’s no window, and the door shuts tight, it’s like something in me reads it as trouble right away. Even if I can tell myself, “Well, people use this elevator all day,” or “That door opens just fine,” I still feel like the space itself is the problem. It’s the being closed in, not seeing an easy way out, that gets to me.
Do you get this same fear in open public places where leaving quickly might be hard?

I’m not sure I’d say that, no. I mean, open public places can be a bother in the usual ways—crowds, walking too far, figuring out where things are—but that doesn’t feel like the same thing to me.

What I’ve noticed is more when something is closed in, you know, when there’s a door shut or the space feels tight. If I’m out in the open, even if it might take me a few minutes to leave, I don’t think I get that same fear in quite the same way. At least, I haven’t really noticed it like I do with the closed spaces.
Do these attacks ever happen when you are not in a closed or tight space?

No, not really—not that I can think of. It’s tied pretty closely to being in that closed-in sort of place. Like I was saying, if I step into a slow elevator, or a small room where the door shuts and I feel like I can’t just get right back out, that’s when my chest kind of jumps on me right away.

It’s not something that just comes over me sitting in my chair at home, or walking outside, or anything like that. It’s more… the minute I’m in a tight space, before I even have a chance to talk myself through it, I get that strong urge to get out. That’s when I stop thinking clearly.
Do you avoid elevators or other closed spaces because of this fear?

Yes, I do, more than I probably like to admit. These days I’ll take the stairs if I can, even if it’s a bit of a climb and I end up moving slower than I used to. I’ll stand there and look at an elevator and think, “Oh, for heaven’s sake, it’s just an elevator,” but then I’ll still turn toward the stairs.

And at the museum, I’ve passed on helping with some of the archive-type jobs, the ones where I’d have to be back in a small room or closed storage area. I feel a bit foolish saying that, because I know it isn’t dangerous in the ordinary sense, but I just don’t like getting myself into a place where I feel shut in.

If I really can’t avoid it, I’ll sometimes ask a friend to stay nearby or wait close to the door, just so I know somebody’s there and I’m not on my own with it. It’s not that I’m proud of doing that, but it makes it easier for me to go through with it.
